<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1134653256">.mw-parser-output .side-box{margin:4px 0;box-sizing:border-box;border:1px solid #aaa;font-size:88%;line-height:1.25em;background-color:#f9f9f9;display:flow-root}.mw-parser-output .side-box-abovebelow,.mw-parser-output .side-box-text{padding:0.25em 0.9em}.mw-parser-output .side-box-image{padding:2px 0 2px 0.9em;text-align:center}.mw-parser-output .side-box-imageright{padding:2px 0.9em 2px 0;text-align:center}@media(min-width:500px){.mw-parser-output .side-box-flex{display:flex;align-items:center}.mw-parser-output .side-box-text{flex:1}}@media(min-width:720px){.mw-parser-output .side-box{width:238px}.mw-parser-output .side-box-right{clear:right;float:right;margin-left:1em}.mw-parser-output .side-box-left{margin-right:1em}}</style><style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1092331828">@media(min-width:720px){.mw-parser-output .contains-special-characters{width:22em}}</style><div class="side-box metadata side-box-right contains-special-characters noprint selfref"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1126788409">
<div class="side-box-flex">
<div class="side-box-image"><span typeof="mw:File"><span><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Urdu_example.svg/40px-Urdu_example.svg.png" decoding="async" width="40" height="40" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Urdu_example.svg/60px-Urdu_example.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Urdu_example.svg/80px-Urdu_example.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="859" data-file-height="857" /></span></span></div>
<div class="side-box-text plainlist">You may need <a href="/wiki/Help:Arabic" title="Help:Arabic">rendering support</a> to display the <a href="/wiki/Urdu_alphabet" title="Urdu alphabet">Urdu text</a> in this article correctly.</div></div>
</div>
<p><b>Pakistan</b> (<a href="/wiki/Urdu_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Urdu language">Urdu</a>: <span lang="ur" dir="rtl"><span class="Nastaliq" dir="rtl" title="Nastaliq" style="font-family: &#39;Jameel Noori Nastaleeq&#39;, &#39;Urdu Typesetting&#39;, &#39;Noto Nastaliq Urdu&#39;, &#39;Noto Nastaliq Urdu Draft&#39;, &#39;Hussaini Nastaleeq&#39;, &#39;AlQalam Taj Nastaleeq&#39;, IranNastaliq, &#39;Awami Nastaliq&#39;, &#39;Awami Nastaliq Beta3&#39;, &#39;Awami Nastaliq Beta2&#39;, &#39;Awami Nastaliq Beta1&#39;, &#39;Nafees Nastaleeq&#39;, &#39;Nafees Nastaleeq v1.01&#39;, &#39;Pak Nastaleeq&#39;, &#39;PDMS_Jauhar&#39;, &#39;Alvi Lahori Nastaleeq&#39;; font-size: 110%; font-style: normal;">پَاکِسْتَان</span></span> <small></small><span title="Representation in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)" class="IPA" lang="ur-Latn-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Hindi_and_Urdu" title="Help:IPA/Hindi and Urdu">[ˈpaːkɪstaːn]</a></span>),<sup id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-19">&#91;d&#93;</a></sup> officially the <b>Islamic Republic of Pakistan</b> (<a href="/wiki/ISO_15919" title="ISO 15919">ISO</a>: <span title="Urdu-language text"><span lang="ur" dir="rtl"><span class="Nastaliq" dir="rtl" title="Nastaliq" style="font-family: &#39;Jameel Noori Nastaleeq&#39;, &#39;Urdu Typesetting&#39;, &#39;Noto Nastaliq Urdu&#39;, &#39;Noto Nastaliq Urdu Draft&#39;, &#39;Hussaini Nastaleeq&#39;, &#39;AlQalam Taj Nastaleeq&#39;, IranNastaliq, &#39;Awami Nastaliq&#39;, &#39;Awami Nastaliq Beta3&#39;, &#39;Awami Nastaliq Beta2&#39;, &#39;Awami Nastaliq Beta1&#39;, &#39;Nafees Nastaleeq&#39;, &#39;Nafees Nastaleeq v1.01&#39;, &#39;Pak Nastaleeq&#39;, &#39;PDMS_Jauhar&#39;, &#39;Alvi Lahori Nastaleeq&#39;; font-size: 110%; font-style: normal;">اِسْلامی
جَمْہُورِیَہ پَاکِسْتَان</span></span></span>, <span title="Urdu-language romanization"><i lang="ur-Latn">islāmi jamhūriyāh pākistān</i></span>), is a country in <a href="/wiki/South_Asia" title="South Asia">South Asia</a>. It is the world's <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population" title="List of countries and dependencies by population">fifth-most populous country</a>, with a population of 241.5 million people, and has the world's <a href="/wiki/Islam_by_country#Countries" title="Islam by country">largest Muslim population</a> as of year 2023.<sup id="cite_ref-2023census_12-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2023census-12">&#91;10&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Islamabad" title="Islamabad">Islamabad</a> is the nation's capital, while <a href="/wiki/Karachi" title="Karachi">Karachi</a> is its largest city and financial centre, followed by <a href="/wiki/Lahore" title="Lahore">Lahore</a> and <a href="/wiki/Faisalabad" title="Faisalabad">Faisalabad</a>. Pakistan is the <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_area" title="List of countries and dependencies by area">33rd-largest country in the world by area</a> and the second-largest in <a href="/wiki/South_Asia" title="South Asia">South Asia</a>, spanning 881,913 square kilometres (340,509 square miles). It has a 1,046-kilometre (650-mile) coastline along the <a href="/wiki/Arabian_Sea" title="Arabian Sea">Arabian Sea</a> and <a href="/wiki/Gulf_of_Oman" title="Gulf of Oman">Gulf of Oman</a> in the south, and is bordered by <a href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</a> to <a href="/wiki/India%E2%80%93Pakistan_border" title="India–Pakistan border">the east</a>, <a href="/wiki/Afghanistan" title="Afghanistan">Afghanistan</a> to <a href="/wiki/Durand_Line" title="Durand Line">the west</a>, <a href="/wiki/Iran" title="Iran">Iran</a> to <a href="/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Pakistan_border" title="Iran–Pakistan border">the southwest</a>, and <a href="/wiki/China" title="China">China</a> to <a href="/wiki/China%E2%80%93Pakistan_border" title="China–Pakistan border">the northeast</a>. It is separated narrowly from <a href="/wiki/Tajikistan" title="Tajikistan">Tajikistan</a> by Afghanistan's <a href="/wiki/Wakhan_Corridor" title="Wakhan Corridor">Wakhan Corridor</a> in the north, and also shares a maritime border with <a href="/wiki/Oman" title="Oman">Oman</a>.
</p><p>Pakistan is the site of <a href="/wiki/History_of_Pakistan" title="History of Pakistan">several ancient cultures</a>, including the 8,500-year-old <a href="/wiki/Neolithic" title="Neolithic">Neolithic</a> site of <a href="/wiki/Mehrgarh" title="Mehrgarh">Mehrgarh</a> in <a href="/wiki/Balochistan,_Pakistan" title="Balochistan, Pakistan">Balochistan</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-20">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup> the <a href="/wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation" class="mw-redirect" title="Indus Valley civilisation">Indus Valley civilisation</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Bronze_Age" title="Bronze Age">Bronze Age</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWright20091–2_21-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWright20091–2-21">&#91;17&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22">&#91;18&#93;</a></sup> and the ancient <a href="/wiki/Gandhara_civilisation" class="mw-redirect" title="Gandhara civilisation">Gandhara civilisation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-23">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup> The regions that comprise the modern state of Pakistan were the realm of multiple empires and dynasties, including the <a href="/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire" title="Achaemenid Empire">Achaemenid</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Maurya_Empire" title="Maurya Empire">Maurya</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Kushan_Empire" title="Kushan Empire">Kushan</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Gupta_Empire" title="Gupta Empire">Gupta</a>;<sup id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24">&#91;20&#93;</a></sup> the <a href="/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate" title="Umayyad Caliphate">Umayyad Caliphate</a> in its southern regions, the <a href="/wiki/Samma_dynasty" title="Samma dynasty">Samma</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Hindu_Shahis" title="Hindu Shahis">Hindu Shahis</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Shah_Miris" class="mw-redirect" title="Shah Miris">Shah Miris</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Ghaznavids" title="Ghaznavids">Ghaznavids</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Delhi_Sultanate" title="Delhi Sultanate">Delhi Sultanate</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Mughal_Empire" title="Mughal Empire">Mughals</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup> and most recently, the <a href="/wiki/British_Raj" title="British Raj">British Raj</a> from 1858 to 1947.
</p><p>Spurred by the <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Movement" title="Pakistan Movement">Pakistan Movement</a>, which sought a homeland for the <a href="/wiki/Muslims" title="Muslims">Muslims</a> of <a href="/wiki/Presidencies_and_provinces_of_British_India" title="Presidencies and provinces of British India">British India</a>, and election victories in 1946 by the <a href="/wiki/All-India_Muslim_League" title="All-India Muslim League">All-India Muslim League</a>, Pakistan gained independence in 1947 after the <a href="/wiki/Partition_of_India" title="Partition of India">Partition of the British Indian Empire</a>, which awarded separate statehood to its Muslim-majority regions and was accompanied by an unparalleled mass migration and loss of life.<sup id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup> Initially a <a href="/wiki/Dominion_of_Pakistan" title="Dominion of Pakistan">Dominion</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations" title="Commonwealth of Nations">British Commonwealth</a>, Pakistan officially drafted <a href="/wiki/Constitution_of_Pakistan" title="Constitution of Pakistan">its constitution</a> in 1956, and emerged as a declared <a href="/wiki/Islamic_republic" title="Islamic republic">Islamic republic</a>. In 1971, the exclave of <a href="/wiki/East_Pakistan" title="East Pakistan">East Pakistan</a> seceded as the new country of <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh" title="Bangladesh">Bangladesh</a> after a <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh_Liberation_War" title="Bangladesh Liberation War">nine-month-long civil war</a>. In the following four decades, Pakistan has been ruled by governments whose descriptions, although complex, commonly alternated between civilian and military, democratic and authoritarian, relatively <a href="/wiki/Secularism_in_Pakistan" title="Secularism in Pakistan">secular</a> and <a href="/wiki/Islamism" title="Islamism">Islamist</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-27">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup> Pakistan elected a civilian government in 2008, and in 2010 adopted a <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_system" title="Parliamentary system">parliamentary system</a> with periodic elections.<sup id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Pakistan is a <a href="/wiki/Middle_power" title="Middle power">middle power</a> nation,<sup id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30">&#91;26&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Buzan2004_32-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Buzan2004-32">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Solomon_33-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Solomon-33">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-34">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup> and has the world's <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_by_number_of_military_and_paramilitary_personnel" title="List of countries by number of military and paramilitary personnel">sixth-largest standing armed forces</a>. It is a declared <a href="/wiki/List_of_states_with_nuclear_weapons" title="List of states with nuclear weapons">nuclear-weapons state</a>, and is ranked amongst the <a href="/wiki/Emerging_and_growth-leading_economies" title="Emerging and growth-leading economies">emerging and growth-leading economies</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-35">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup> with a large and rapidly-growing middle class.<sup id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-36">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup> Pakistan's political history since independence has been characterised by periods of significant economic and military growth as well as those of political and economic instability. It is an <a href="/wiki/Ethnic_groups_in_Pakistan" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethnic groups in Pakistan">ethnically</a> and <a href="/wiki/Languages_of_Pakistan" title="Languages of Pakistan">linguistically</a> diverse country, with similarly diverse <a href="/wiki/Geography_of_Pakistan" title="Geography of Pakistan">geography</a> and <a href="/wiki/Wildlife_of_Pakistan" title="Wildlife of Pakistan">wildlife</a>. The country continues to face challenges, including <a href="/wiki/Poverty_in_Pakistan" title="Poverty in Pakistan">poverty</a>, <a href="/wiki/Literate_Pakistan_Foundation" class="mw-redirect" title="Literate Pakistan Foundation">illiteracy</a>, <a href="/wiki/Corruption_in_Pakistan" title="Corruption in Pakistan">corruption</a> and <a href="/wiki/Terrorism_in_Pakistan" title="Terrorism in Pakistan">terrorism</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup> Pakistan is a member of the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations" title="United Nations">United Nations</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Shanghai_Cooperation_Organisation" title="Shanghai Cooperation Organisation">Shanghai Cooperation Organisation</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation" title="Organisation of Islamic Cooperation">Organisation of Islamic Cooperation</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations" title="Commonwealth of Nations">Commonwealth of Nations</a>, the <a href="/wiki/South_Asian_Association_for_Regional_Cooperation" title="South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation">South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Islamic_Military_Counter_Terrorism_Coalition" title="Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition">Islamic Military Counter-Terrorism Coalition</a>, and is designated as a <a href="/wiki/Major_non-NATO_ally" title="Major non-NATO ally">major non-NATO ally</a> by the <a href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</a>.
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Etymology">Etymology</span></h2>
<p>The name <i>Pakistan</i> was coined by <a href="/wiki/Choudhry_Rahmat_Ali" title="Choudhry Rahmat Ali">Choudhry Rahmat Ali</a>, a <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Movement" title="Pakistan Movement">Pakistan Movement</a> activist, who in January 1933 first published it (originally as "Pakstan") in a pamphlet <i><a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Declaration" title="Pakistan Declaration">Now or Never</a></i>, using it as an <a href="/wiki/Acronym" title="Acronym">acronym</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-38">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup> Rahmat Ali explained: "It is composed of letters taken from the names of all our homelands, Indian and Asian, <a href="/wiki/Punjab_Province_(British_India)" title="Punjab Province (British India)"><i>P</i>anjab</a>, <a href="/wiki/North-West_Frontier_Province_(1901%E2%80%932010)" class="mw-redirect" title="North-West Frontier Province (1901–2010)"><i>A</i>fghania</a>, <a href="/wiki/Jammu_and_Kashmir_(princely_state)" title="Jammu and Kashmir (princely state)"><i>K</i>ashmir</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sind_Division" title="Sind Division"><i>S</i>indh</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Baluchistan_Agency" title="Baluchistan Agency">Baluchis<i>tan</i></a>." He added that "Pakistan is both a <a href="/wiki/Persian_language" title="Persian language">Persian</a> and <a href="/wiki/Urdu" title="Urdu">Urdu</a> word... It means the land of the Paks, the spiritually pure and clean."<sup id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-39">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup> Etymologists note that <span lang="fa"><a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D9%BE%D8%A7%DA%A9#Persian" class="extiw" title="wikt:پاک">پاک</a></span> <span title="Persian-language romanization"><i lang="fa-Latn">pāk</i></span>, is 'pure' in Persian and <a href="/wiki/Pashto" title="Pashto">Pashto</a><sup id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup> and the Persian suffix <span lang="fa"><a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D9%80%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%A7%D9%86#Persian" class="extiw" title="wikt:ـستان">ـستان</a></span> <span title="Persian-language romanization"><i lang="fa-Latn"><a href="/wiki/-stan" title="-stan">-stan</a></i></span> means 'land' or 'place of'.<sup id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-44">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Rahmat Ali's concept of Pakistan only related to the north-west area of the Indian subcontinent. He also proposed the name "Banglastan" for the Muslim areas of <a href="/wiki/Bengal" title="Bengal">Bengal</a> and "Osmanistan" for <a href="/wiki/Hyderabad_State" title="Hyderabad State">Hyderabad State</a>, as well as a political federation between the three.<sup id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-46">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="History">History</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/History_of_Pakistan" title="History of Pakistan">History of Pakistan</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation" class="mw-redirect" title="Indus Valley civilisation">Indus Valley civilisation</a>, <a href="/wiki/Vedic_period" title="Vedic period">Vedic period</a>, <a href="/wiki/Maurya_Empire" title="Maurya Empire">Maurya Empire</a>, <a href="/wiki/Indo-Greek_Kingdom" title="Indo-Greek Kingdom">Indo-Greek Kingdom</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gupta_Empire" title="Gupta Empire">Gupta Empire</a>, <a href="/wiki/Kushan_Empire" title="Kushan Empire">Kushan Empire</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sikh_Empire" title="Sikh Empire">Sikh Empire</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Mughal_Empire" title="Mughal Empire">Mughal Empire</a></div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Outline_of_South_Asian_history" title="Outline of South Asian history">Outline of South Asian history</a></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Indus_Valley_Civilization">Indus Valley Civilization</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mohenjo-daro_Priesterk%C3%B6nig.jpeg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Mohenjo-daro_Priesterk%C3%B6nig.jpeg/170px-Mohenjo-daro_Priesterk%C3%B6nig.jpeg" decoding="async" width="170" height="219" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Mohenjo-daro_Priesterk%C3%B6nig.jpeg/255px-Mohenjo-daro_Priesterk%C3%B6nig.jpeg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Mohenjo-daro_Priesterk%C3%B6nig.jpeg/340px-Mohenjo-daro_Priesterk%C3%B6nig.jpeg 2x" data-file-width="584" data-file-height="754" /></a><figcaption><i><a href="/wiki/Priest-king_(sculpture)" class="mw-redirect" title="Priest-king (sculpture)">Priest-King</a></i> from <a href="/wiki/Mohenjo-Daro" class="mw-redirect" title="Mohenjo-Daro">Mohenjo-Daro</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;">&#8201;2500 BCE</span>)</figcaption></figure>
<p>Some of the earliest ancient human civilisations in <a href="/wiki/South_Asia" title="South Asia">South Asia</a> originated from areas encompassing present-day Pakistan.<sup id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> The earliest known inhabitants in the region were <a href="/wiki/Soanian" title="Soanian">Soanian</a> during the <a href="/wiki/Lower_Paleolithic" title="Lower Paleolithic">Lower Paleolithic</a>, of whom stone tools have been found in the <a href="/wiki/Soan_Valley" class="mw-redirect" title="Soan Valley">Soan Valley</a> of <a href="/wiki/Punjab,_Pakistan" title="Punjab, Pakistan">Punjab</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Indus_River" title="Indus River">Indus region</a>, which covers most of present day Pakistan, was the site of several successive ancient cultures including the Neolithic Mehrgarh<sup id="cite_ref-vipul_49-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vipul-49">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup> and the Bronze Age <a href="/wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation" class="mw-redirect" title="Indus Valley civilisation">Indus Valley civilisation</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWright2009_50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWright2009-50">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup> (2,800–1,800&#160;BCE) at <a href="/wiki/Harappa" title="Harappa">Harappa</a> and <a href="/wiki/Mohenjo-Daro" class="mw-redirect" title="Mohenjo-Daro">Mohenjo-Daro</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-52">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Vedic_Period">Vedic Period</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Gandhara_Buddha_(tnm).jpeg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Gandhara_Buddha_%28tnm%29.jpeg/170px-Gandhara_Buddha_%28tnm%29.jpeg" decoding="async" width="170" height="282" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Gandhara_Buddha_%28tnm%29.jpeg/255px-Gandhara_Buddha_%28tnm%29.jpeg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Gandhara_Buddha_%28tnm%29.jpeg/340px-Gandhara_Buddha_%28tnm%29.jpeg 2x" data-file-width="1746" data-file-height="2894" /></a><figcaption><i><a href="/wiki/Standing_Buddha" class="mw-redirect" title="Standing Buddha">Standing Buddha</a></i> from <a href="/wiki/Gandhara" title="Gandhara">Gandhara</a> (1st–2nd century CE)</figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Vedic_period" title="Vedic period">Vedic period</a> (1500–500&#160;BCE) was characterised by an <a href="/wiki/Indo-Aryan_peoples" title="Indo-Aryan peoples">Indo-Aryan</a> culture; during this period the <a href="/wiki/Vedas" title="Vedas">Vedas</a>, the oldest scriptures associated with <a href="/wiki/Hinduism" title="Hinduism">Hinduism</a>, were composed, and this culture later became well established in the region.<sup id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Multan" title="Multan">Multan</a> was an important Hindu pilgrimage centre.<sup id="cite_ref-taxila_54-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-taxila-54">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup> The Vedic civilisation flourished in the ancient <a href="/wiki/Gandhara" title="Gandhara">Gandhāran</a> city of Takṣaśilā, now <a href="/wiki/Taxila" title="Taxila">Taxila</a> in the Punjab, which was founded around 1000 BCE.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAllchinAllchin1988314_55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllchinAllchin1988314-55">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-vipul_49-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vipul-49">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Classical_Period">Classical Period</span></h3>
<p>The western regions of Pakistan <a href="/wiki/Achaemenid_conquest_of_the_Indus_Valley" title="Achaemenid conquest of the Indus Valley">became part</a> of <a href="/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire" title="Achaemenid Empire">Achaemenid Empire</a>  around 519&#160;BCE. In 326&#160;BCE, <a href="/wiki/Alexander_the_Great" title="Alexander the Great">Alexander the Great</a> conquered the region by defeating various local rulers, most notably, the King <a href="/wiki/Porus" title="Porus">Porus</a>, at <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Hydaspes" class="mw-redirect" title="Battle of Hydaspes">Jhelum</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup> It was followed by the <a href="/wiki/Maurya_Empire" title="Maurya Empire">Maurya Empire</a>, founded by <a href="/wiki/Chandragupta_Maurya" title="Chandragupta Maurya">Chandragupta Maurya</a> and extended by <a href="/wiki/Ashoka_the_Great" class="mw-redirect" title="Ashoka the Great">Ashoka the Great</a>, until 185&#160;BCE. The <a href="/wiki/Indo-Greek_Kingdom" title="Indo-Greek Kingdom">Indo-Greek Kingdom</a> founded by <a href="/wiki/Demetrius_I_of_Bactria" title="Demetrius I of Bactria">Demetrius of Bactria</a> (180–165&#160;BCE) included Gandhara and Punjab and reached its greatest extent under <a href="/wiki/Menander_I" title="Menander I">Menander</a> (165–150&#160;BCE), prospering the <a href="/wiki/Greco-Buddhism" title="Greco-Buddhism">Greco-Buddhist</a> culture in the region.<sup id="cite_ref-vipul_49-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vipul-49">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-57" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-57">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup> Taxila had one of the earliest universities and centres of higher education in the world, which was established during the late Vedic period in the 6th century BCE.<sup id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-59">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup> The school consisted of several monasteries without large dormitories or lecture halls where the religious instruction was provided on an individualistic basis.<sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_59-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-59">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup> The ancient university was documented by the invading forces of Alexander the Great and was also recorded by Chinese pilgrims in the 4th or 5th century CE.<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>At its zenith, the <a href="/wiki/Rai_Dynasty" class="mw-redirect" title="Rai Dynasty">Rai Dynasty</a> (489–632&#160;CE) ruled <a href="/wiki/Sindh" title="Sindh">Sindh</a> and the surrounding territories.<sup id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Islamic_conquest">Islamic conquest</span></h3>
<p>The Arab conqueror <a href="/wiki/Muhammad_ibn_Qasim" class="mw-redirect" title="Muhammad ibn Qasim">Muhammad ibn Qasim</a> conquered Sindh in 711&#160;CE.<sup id="cite_ref-Information_of_Pakistan_62-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Information_of_Pakistan-62">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup> The Pakistan government's official chronology claims this as the time when the foundation of Pakistan was laid<sup id="cite_ref-Information_of_Pakistan_62-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Information_of_Pakistan-62">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup> but the concept of <i>Pakistan</i> arrived in the 19th century. The Early Medieval period (642–1219&#160;CE) witnessed the spread of <a href="/wiki/Islam" title="Islam">Islam</a> in the region. During this period, <a href="/wiki/Sufi" class="mw-redirect" title="Sufi">Sufi</a> <a href="/wiki/Dawah" title="Dawah">missionaries</a> played a pivotal role in converting a majority of the regional Buddhist and Hindu population to Islam.<sup id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-65">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> Upon the defeat of the <a href="/wiki/Turk_Shahis" title="Turk Shahis">Turk</a> and <a href="/wiki/Hindu_Shahi" class="mw-redirect" title="Hindu Shahi">Hindu Shahi</a> dynasties which governed the <a href="/wiki/Kabul_Valley" class="mw-redirect" title="Kabul Valley">Kabul Valley</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gandhara" title="Gandhara">Gandhara</a> (present-day Khyber Pakhtunkwa), and western Punjab in the 7th to 11th centuries CE, <a href="/wiki/Muslim_conquest_in_the_Indian_subcontinent" class="mw-redirect" title="Muslim conquest in the Indian subcontinent">several successive Muslim empires</a> ruled over the region, including the <a href="/wiki/Ghaznavids" title="Ghaznavids">Ghaznavid Empire</a> (975–1187&#160;CE), the <a href="/wiki/Ghorid" class="mw-redirect" title="Ghorid">Ghorid</a> Kingdom, and the <a href="/wiki/Delhi_Sultanate" title="Delhi Sultanate">Delhi Sultanate</a> (1206–1526&#160;CE). The <a href="/wiki/Lodi_dynasty" title="Lodi dynasty">Lodi dynasty</a>, the last of the Delhi Sultanate, was replaced by the Mughal Empire (1526–1857&#160;CE).
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Badshahi_Masjid_-_Side_View.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Badshahi_Masjid_-_Side_View.jpg/220px-Badshahi_Masjid_-_Side_View.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Badshahi_Masjid_-_Side_View.jpg/330px-Badshahi_Masjid_-_Side_View.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Badshahi_Masjid_-_Side_View.jpg/440px-Badshahi_Masjid_-_Side_View.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5078" data-file-height="3385" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Badshahi_Mosque" title="Badshahi Mosque">Badshahi Mosque</a>, <a href="/wiki/Lahore" title="Lahore">Lahore</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The Mughals introduced Persian literature and high culture, establishing the roots of <a href="/wiki/Indo-Persian_culture" title="Indo-Persian culture">Indo-Persian culture</a> in the region.<sup id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-66">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup> In the region of modern-day Pakistan, key cities during the Mughal period were <a href="/wiki/Lahore" title="Lahore">Lahore</a> and <a href="/wiki/Thatta" title="Thatta">Thatta</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup> both of which were chosen as the site of impressive <a href="/wiki/Mughal_architecture" title="Mughal architecture">Mughal buildings</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup> In the early 16th century, the region remained under the <a href="/wiki/Mughal_Empire" title="Mughal Empire">Mughal Empire</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the 18th century, the slow disintegration of the Mughal Empire was hastened by the emergence of the rival powers of the <a href="/wiki/Maratha_Confederacy" class="mw-redirect" title="Maratha Confederacy">Maratha Confederacy</a> and later the <a href="/wiki/Sikh_Empire" title="Sikh Empire">Sikh Empire</a>, as well as invasions by <a href="/wiki/Nader_Shah" title="Nader Shah">Nader Shah</a> from Iran in 1739 and the <a href="/wiki/Durrani_Empire" title="Durrani Empire">Durrani Empire</a> of Afghanistan in 1759. The growing political power of the British in Bengal had not yet reached the territories of modern Pakistan.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Colonial_period">Colonial period</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/British_India" class="mw-redirect" title="British India">British India</a>, <a href="/wiki/Aligarh_Movement" title="Aligarh Movement">Aligarh Movement</a>, <a href="/wiki/British_Raj" title="British Raj">British Raj</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Two-nation_theory" title="Two-nation theory">Two-nation theory</a></div>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti">.mw-parser-output .tmulti .multiimageinner{display:flex;flex-direction:column}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .thumbcaption{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow>.thumbcaption{text-align:center}}</style><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:348px;max-width:348px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:172px;max-width:172px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Sir_Syed1.jpg" title="Syed Ahmad Khan">Syed Ahmad Khan</a> (1817–1898), whose <a href="/wiki/Two-nation_theory" title="Two-nation theory">vision</a> formed the basis of Pakistan</div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:172px;max-width:172px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Jinnah1945b.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Muhammad Ali Jinnah (1876–1948) served as //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Jinnah1945b.jpg/340px-Jinnah1945b.jpg 2x" data-file-width="650" data-file-height="853" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Muhammad_Ali_Jinnah" title="Muhammad Ali Jinnah">Muhammad Ali Jinnah</a> (1876–1948) served as Pakistan's first Governor-General and the leader of the <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Movement" title="Pakistan Movement">Pakistan Movement</a>.</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>None of the territory of modern Pakistan was ruled by the British until 1839 when <a href="/wiki/Karachi" title="Karachi">Karachi</a>, a small fishing village ruled by <a href="/wiki/Talpur_dynasty" title="Talpur dynasty">Talpurs</a> of <a href="/wiki/Sindh" title="Sindh">Sindh</a> with a mud fort guarding the harbour, was <a href="/wiki/History_of_Karachi#Company_rule" title="History of Karachi">taken</a>, and held as an enclave with a port and <a href="/wiki/Karachi_Cantonment" title="Karachi Cantonment">military base</a> for the <a href="/wiki/First_Afghan_War" class="mw-redirect" title="First Afghan War">First Afghan War</a> that soon followed. The rest of <a href="/wiki/Sindh" title="Sindh">Sindh</a> was taken in 1843, and in the following decades, first the <a href="/wiki/British_East_India_Company" class="mw-redirect" title="British East India Company">East India Company</a>, and then after the post-<a href="/wiki/Sepoy_Mutiny" class="mw-redirect" title="Sepoy Mutiny">Sepoy Mutiny</a> (1857–1858) direct rule of <a href="/wiki/Queen_Victoria" title="Queen Victoria">Queen Victoria</a> of the <a href="/wiki/British_Empire" title="British Empire">British Empire</a>, took over most of the country partly through wars, and also treaties. The main wars were that against the <a href="/wiki/Baloch_people" title="Baloch people">Baloch</a> <a href="/wiki/Talpur_dynasty" title="Talpur dynasty">Talpur dynasty</a>, ended by the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Miani" title="Battle of Miani">Battle of Miani</a> (1843) in Sindh, the <a href="/wiki/Anglo-Sikh_War_(disambiguation)" class="mw-redirect mw-disambig" title="Anglo-Sikh War (disambiguation)">Anglo-Sikh Wars</a> (1845–1849) and the <a href="/wiki/Anglo-Afghan_War" title="Anglo-Afghan War">Anglo-Afghan Wars</a> (1839–1919). By 1893, all modern Pakistan was part of the <a href="/wiki/British_Indian_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="British Indian Empire">British Indian Empire</a>, and remained so until independence in 1947.
</p><p>Under the British, modern Pakistan was mostly divided into the <a href="/wiki/Sind_Division" title="Sind Division">Sind Division</a>, <a href="/wiki/Punjab_Province_(British_India)" title="Punjab Province (British India)">Punjab Province</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Baluchistan_Agency" title="Baluchistan Agency">Baluchistan Agency</a>. There were various <a href="/wiki/Princely_state" title="Princely state">princely states</a>, of which the largest was <a href="/wiki/Bahawalpur_(princely_state)" title="Bahawalpur (princely state)">Bahawalpur</a>.
</p><p>A <a href="/wiki/Indian_Rebellion_of_1857" title="Indian Rebellion of 1857">rebellion</a> in 1857 called the <a href="/wiki/Sepoy_mutiny" class="mw-redirect" title="Sepoy mutiny">Sepoy mutiny</a> of <a href="/wiki/Bengal" title="Bengal">Bengal</a> was the region's major armed struggle against the British.<sup id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-70">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup> Divergence in the <a href="/wiki/Hindu%E2%80%93Islamic_relations" title="Hindu–Islamic relations">relationship</a> between Hinduism and Islam created a major rift in <a href="/wiki/British_Raj" title="British Raj">British India</a> that led to motivated <a href="/wiki/Violence_against_Muslims_in_India" class="mw-redirect" title="Violence against Muslims in India">religious violence in British India</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-71">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Hindi%E2%80%93Urdu_controversy" title="Hindi–Urdu controversy">language controversy</a> further escalated the tensions between Hindus and Muslims.<sup id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-72">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Bengali_Renaissance" title="Bengali Renaissance">Hindu renaissance</a> witnessed an awakening of intellectualism in traditional <a href="/wiki/Hinduism" title="Hinduism">Hinduism</a> and saw the emergence of more assertive influence in the social and political spheres in British India.<sup id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-73">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup> A <a href="/wiki/Aligarh_Movement" title="Aligarh Movement">Muslim intellectual movement</a>, founded by Sir <a href="/wiki/Syed_Ahmed_Khan" class="mw-redirect" title="Syed Ahmed Khan">Syed Ahmed Khan</a> to counter the Hindu renaissance, envisioned as well as advocated for the <a href="/wiki/Two-nation_theory" title="Two-nation theory">two-nation theory</a><sup id="cite_ref-congress_74-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-congress-74">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup> and led to the creation of the <a href="/wiki/All-India_Muslim_League" title="All-India Muslim League">All-India Muslim League</a> in 1906. In contrast to the <a href="/wiki/Indian_National_Congress" title="Indian National Congress">Indian National Congress</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Anti-British_sentiment" title="Anti-British sentiment">anti-British</a> efforts, the Muslim League was a <a href="/wiki/Anglomania" class="mw-redirect" title="Anglomania">pro-British</a> movement whose political program <a href="/wiki/British_heritage_of_Pakistan" class="mw-redirect" title="British heritage of Pakistan">inherited the British values</a> that would shape Pakistan's future <a href="/wiki/Pakistani_society" class="mw-redirect" title="Pakistani society">civil society</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-75">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup> The largely non-violent independence struggle led by the <a href="/wiki/Indian_National_Congress" title="Indian National Congress">Indian National Congress</a> under the leadership of <a href="/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi" title="Mahatma Gandhi">Mahatma Gandhi</a> engaged millions of protesters in mass campaigns of <a href="/wiki/Indian_independence_movement" title="Indian independence movement">civil disobedience</a> in the 1920s and 1930s against the <a href="/wiki/British_Empire" title="British Empire">British Empire</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-76">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Brookings_Institution_Press_77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brookings_Institution_Press-77">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Clock_Tower_Faisalabad_by_Usman_Nadeem.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Clock_Tower_Faisalabad_by_Usman_Nadeem.jpg/220px-Clock_Tower_Faisalabad_by_Usman_Nadeem.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="155" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Clock_Tower_Faisalabad_by_Usman_Nadeem.jpg/330px-Clock_Tower_Faisalabad_by_Usman_Nadeem.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Clock_Tower_Faisalabad_by_Usman_Nadeem.jpg/440px-Clock_Tower_Faisalabad_by_Usman_Nadeem.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4920" data-file-height="3456" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Clock_Tower,_Faisalabad" title="Clock Tower, Faisalabad">Clock Tower, Faisalabad</a>, built by the British government in the 19th century</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Muslim League slowly rose to mass popularity in the 1930s amid fears of under-representation and neglect by the British of the <a href="/wiki/Indian_Muslims" class="mw-redirect" title="Indian Muslims">Indian Muslims</a> in <a href="/wiki/Indian_politics" class="mw-redirect" title="Indian politics">politics</a>. In his presidential address of 29 December 1930, <a href="/wiki/Muhammad_Iqbal" title="Muhammad Iqbal">Allama Iqbal</a> called for "the amalgamation of <a href="/wiki/Northwestern_India" class="mw-redirect" title="Northwestern India">North-West</a> Muslim-majority Indian states" consisting of <a href="/wiki/Punjab_Province_(British_India)" title="Punjab Province (British India)">Punjab</a>, <a href="/wiki/North-West_Frontier_Province_(1901%E2%80%9355)" class="mw-redirect" title="North-West Frontier Province (1901–55)">North-West Frontier Province</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sind_Province_(1936%E2%80%9355)" class="mw-redirect" title="Sind Province (1936–55)">Sind</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Baluchistan_(Chief_Commissioner%27s_Province)" title="Baluchistan (Chief Commissioner&#39;s Province)">Baluchistan</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-78" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-78">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup> The perceived neglect of Muslim interests by Congress led British <a href="/wiki/1937_Indian_provincial_elections" title="1937 Indian provincial elections">provincial governments</a> during the period of 1937–39 convinced <a href="/wiki/Muhammad_Ali_Jinnah" title="Muhammad Ali Jinnah">Muhammad Ali Jinnah</a>, the founder of Pakistan to espouse the two-nation theory and led the Muslim League to adopt the <a href="/wiki/Lahore_Resolution" title="Lahore Resolution">Lahore Resolution</a> of 1940 presented by <a href="/wiki/Sher-e-Bangla" class="mw-redirect" title="Sher-e-Bangla">Sher-e-Bangla</a> <a href="/wiki/A.K._Fazlul_Haque" class="mw-redirect" title="A.K. Fazlul Haque">A.K. Fazlul Haque</a>, popularly known as the Pakistan Resolution.<sup id="cite_ref-congress_74-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-congress-74">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup> In <a href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</a>, Jinnah and <a href="/wiki/British_education" class="mw-redirect" title="British education">British-educated</a> <a href="/wiki/Founding_Fathers_of_Pakistan" class="mw-redirect" title="Founding Fathers of Pakistan">founding fathers</a> in the Muslim League supported the United Kingdom's <a href="/wiki/United_Kingdom_in_World_War_II" class="mw-redirect" title="United Kingdom in World War II">war efforts</a>, countering opposition against it whilst working towards Sir Syed's <a href="/wiki/Two-nation_theory" title="Two-nation theory">vision</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-79" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-79">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Pakistan_Movement">Pakistan Movement</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Movement" title="Pakistan Movement">Pakistan Movement</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_Islamic_Republic_of_Pakistan" class="mw-redirect" title="History of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan">History of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Indian_independence_movement" title="Indian independence movement">Indian independence movement</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Partition_of_India" title="Partition of India">Partition of India</a></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/1946_Indian_provincial_elections" title="1946 Indian provincial elections">1946 elections</a> resulted in the Muslim League winning 90&#160;percent of the seats reserved for Muslims. Thus, the 1946 election was seen as a plebiscite in which the Indian Muslims were to vote on the creation of Pakistan, a plebiscite won by the Muslim League. This victory was assisted by the support given to the Muslim League by the support of the landowners of Sindh and Punjab. The Indian National Congress, which initially denied the Muslim League's claim of being the sole representative of Indian Muslims, was now forced to recognise the fact.<sup id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-80">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-81">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup> The British had no alternative except to take Jinnah's views into account as he had emerged as the sole spokesperson of the entirety of British India's Muslims. However, the British <a href="/wiki/Opposition_to_the_partition_of_India" class="mw-redirect" title="Opposition to the partition of India">did not want colonial India to be partitioned</a>, and in one last effort to prevent it, they devised the <a href="/wiki/Cabinet_Mission_Plan" class="mw-redirect" title="Cabinet Mission Plan">Cabinet Mission plan</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-82">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As the cabinet mission failed, the British government announced its intention to end the British Rule in 1946–47.<sup id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-83">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Indian_nationalism" title="Indian nationalism">Nationalists</a> in British India—including <a href="/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru" title="Jawaharlal Nehru">Jawaharlal Nehru</a> and <a href="/wiki/Abul_Kalam_Azad" class="mw-redirect" title="Abul Kalam Azad">Abul Kalam Azad</a> of Congress, Jinnah of the <a href="/wiki/All-India_Muslim_League" title="All-India Muslim League">All-India Muslim League</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Master_Tara_Singh" class="mw-redirect" title="Master Tara Singh">Master Tara Singh</a> representing the Sikhs—agreed to the proposed terms of transfer of power and independence in June 1947 with the <a href="/wiki/Governor-General_of_India" title="Governor-General of India">Viceroy of India</a>, <a href="/wiki/Louis_Mountbatten,_1st_Earl_Mountbatten_of_Burma" title="Louis Mountbatten, 1st Earl Mountbatten of Burma">Lord Mountbatten of Burma</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-jinnah_84-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-jinnah-84">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup> As the United Kingdom agreed to the <a href="/wiki/Partition_of_India" title="Partition of India">partitioning of India</a> in 1947, the modern state of Pakistan was established on <a href="/wiki/Fourteenth_of_August" class="mw-redirect" title="Fourteenth of August">14 August 1947</a> <span style="font-size:85%;">(27th of <a href="/wiki/Ramadan" title="Ramadan">Ramadan</a> in 1366 of the <a href="/wiki/Islamic_Calendar" class="mw-redirect" title="Islamic Calendar">Islamic Calendar</a>)</span>, amalgamating the <a href="/wiki/Islam_in_India" title="Islam in India">Muslim-majority</a> eastern and northwestern regions of <a href="/wiki/British_India" class="mw-redirect" title="British India">British India</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Brookings_Institution_Press_77-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brookings_Institution_Press-77">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup> It comprised the provinces of <a href="/wiki/Balochistan_(Pakistan)" class="mw-redirect" title="Balochistan (Pakistan)">Balochistan</a>, <a href="/wiki/East_Bengal" title="East Bengal">East Bengal</a>, the <a href="/wiki/North-West_Frontier_Province_(1901%E2%80%931955)" class="mw-redirect" title="North-West Frontier Province (1901–1955)">North-West Frontier Province</a>, <a href="/wiki/Punjab,_Pakistan" title="Punjab, Pakistan">West Punjab</a>, and Sindh.<sup id="cite_ref-congress_74-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-congress-74">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-jinnah_84-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-jinnah-84">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the riots that accompanied the partition in Punjab Province, it is believed that between 200,000 and 2,000,000<sup id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup> people were killed in what some have described as a retributive genocide between the religions<sup id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-86">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup> while 50,000 Muslim women were <a href="/wiki/Violence_against_women_during_the_partition_of_India" class="mw-redirect" title="Violence against women during the partition of India">abducted and raped</a> by Hindu and Sikh men, 33,000 Hindu and Sikh women also experienced the same fate at the hands of Muslims.<sup id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-87">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup> Around 6.5&#160;million Muslims moved from India to West Pakistan and 4.7&#160;million Hindus and Sikhs moved from West Pakistan to India.<sup id="cite_ref-ECM_88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ECM-88">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup> It was the largest mass migration in human history.<sup id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-89">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup> A subsequent dispute over the <a href="/wiki/Princely_state" title="Princely state">princely state</a> of <a href="/wiki/Jammu_and_Kashmir_(princely_state)" title="Jammu and Kashmir (princely state)">Jammu and Kashmir</a> eventually sparked the <a href="/wiki/Indo-Pakistani_War_of_1947%E2%80%931948" title="Indo-Pakistani War of 1947–1948">Indo-Pakistani War of 1947–1948</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-90" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-90">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Independence_and_modern_Pakistan">Independence and modern Pakistan</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Dominion_of_Pakistan" title="Dominion of Pakistan">Dominion of Pakistan</a> and <a href="/wiki/History_of_Pakistan" title="History of Pakistan">History of Pakistan</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Monarchy_of_Pakistan" title="Monarchy of Pakistan">Monarchy of Pakistan</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Queen_Elizabeth_II_official_portrait_for_1959_tour_(retouched)_(cropped)_(3-to-4_aspect_ratio).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Queen_Elizabeth_II_official_portrait_for_1959_tour_%28retouched%29_%28cropped%29_%283-to-4_aspect_ratio%29.jpg/180px-Queen_Elizabeth_II_official_portrait_for_1959_tour_%28retouched%29_%28cropped%29_%283-to-4_aspect_ratio%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="240" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Queen_Elizabeth_II_official_portrait_for_1959_tour_%28retouched%29_%28cropped%29_%283-to-4_aspect_ratio%29.jpg/270px-Queen_Elizabeth_II_official_portrait_for_1959_tour_%28retouched%29_%28cropped%29_%283-to-4_aspect_ratio%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Queen_Elizabeth_II_official_portrait_for_1959_tour_%28retouched%29_%28cropped%29_%283-to-4_aspect_ratio%29.jpg/360px-Queen_Elizabeth_II_official_portrait_for_1959_tour_%28retouched%29_%28cropped%29_%283-to-4_aspect_ratio%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="739" data-file-height="985" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II" class="mw-redirect" title="Queen Elizabeth II">Queen Elizabeth II</a> was the last monarch of independent Pakistan, before it became a republic in 1956.</figcaption></figure>
<p>After <a href="/wiki/Creation_of_Pakistan" class="mw-redirect" title="Creation of Pakistan">independence</a> in 1947, Jinnah, the <a href="/wiki/Party_chair" title="Party chair">President</a> of the Muslim League, became the nation's first <a href="/wiki/Governor-General_of_Pakistan" title="Governor-General of Pakistan">Governor-General</a> as well as the first <a href="/wiki/Speaker_of_the_National_Assembly_of_Pakistan" title="Speaker of the National Assembly of Pakistan">President-Speaker</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Pakistan" title="Parliament of Pakistan">Parliament</a>, but he died of tuberculosis on 11 September 1948.<sup id="cite_ref-91" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-91">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup> Meanwhile, Pakistan's founding fathers agreed to appoint <a href="/wiki/Liaquat_Ali_Khan" title="Liaquat Ali Khan">Liaquat Ali Khan</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Secretary_General" class="mw-redirect" title="Secretary General">secretary-general</a> of the <a href="/wiki/All-India_Muslim_League" title="All-India Muslim League">party</a>, the nation's <a href="/wiki/List_of_Prime_Ministers_of_Pakistan" class="mw-redirect" title="List of Prime Ministers of Pakistan">first</a> <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Pakistan" title="Prime Minister of Pakistan">Prime Minister</a>. From 1947 to 1956, <a href="/wiki/Monarchy_of_Pakistan" title="Monarchy of Pakistan">Pakistan was a monarchy</a> within the Commonwealth of Nations, and had two monarchs before it became a republic.<sup id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The creation of Pakistan was never fully accepted by many British leaders, among them <a href="/wiki/Louis_Mountbatten,_1st_Earl_Mountbatten_of_Burma" title="Louis Mountbatten, 1st Earl Mountbatten of Burma">Lord Mountbatten</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup> Mountbatten clearly expressed his lack of support and faith in the Muslim League's idea of Pakistan.<sup id="cite_ref-94" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-94">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup> Jinnah refused Mountbatten's offer to serve as <a href="/wiki/Governor-General_of_Pakistan" title="Governor-General of Pakistan">Governor-General of Pakistan</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-95" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-95">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup> When Mountbatten was asked by Collins and Lapierre if he would have sabotaged Pakistan had he known that Jinnah was dying of tuberculosis, he replied 'most probably'.<sup id="cite_ref-96" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-96">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><span><video id="mwe_player_1" poster="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Pakistan.ogv/220px--Pakistan.ogv.jpg" controls="" preload="none" class="mw-file-element" width="220" height="165" data-durationhint="1069" data-mwtitle="Pakistan.ogv" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons" resource="/wiki/File:Pakistan.ogv"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7a/Pakistan.ogv" type="video/ogg; <style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1062260506">.mw-parser-output .quotebox{background-color:#F9F9F9;border:1px solid #aaa;box-sizing:border-box;padding:10px;font-size:88%;max-width:100%}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatleft{margin:.5em 1.4em .8em 0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatright{margin:.5em 0 .8em 1.4em}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.centered{overflow:hidden;position:relative;margin:.5em auto .8em auto}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatleft span,.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatright span{font-style:inherit}.mw-parser-output .quotebox>blockquote{margin:0;padding:0;border-left:0;font-family:inherit;font-size:inherit}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-title{background-color:#F9F9F9;text-align:center;font-size:110%;font-weight:bold}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote>:first-child{margin-top:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote:last-child>:last-child{margin-bottom:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote.quoted:before{font-family:"Times New Roman",serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:large;color:gray;content:" “ ";vertical-align:-45%;line-height:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote.quoted:after{font-family:"Times New Roman",serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:large;color:gray;content:" ” ";line-height:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .left-aligned{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .right-aligned{text-align:right}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .center-aligned{text-align:center}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .quote-title,.mw-parser-output .quotebox .quotebox-quote{display:block}.mw-parser-output .quotebox cite{display:block;font-style:normal}@media screen and (max-width:640px){.mw-parser-output .quotebox{width:100%!important;margin:0 0 .8em!important;float:none!important}}</style><div class="quotebox pullquote floatright" style="width:25em; border-width: 1px; background-color: #c6dbf7;">
<blockquote class="quotebox-quote left-aligned" style="">
<p>"You are free; you are free to go to your temples, you are free to go to your mosques or to any other place or worship in this State of Pakistan. You may belong to any religion or caste or creed&#160;– that has nothing to do with the business of the State."
</p>
</blockquote>
<p><cite class="left-aligned" style="">—<a href="/wiki/Muhammad_Ali_Jinnah" title="Muhammad Ali Jinnah">Muhammad Ali Jinnah</a>'s first speech to the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan<sup id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-97">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup></cite>
</p>
</div>
<p>Maulana <a href="/wiki/Shabbir_Ahmad_Usmani" title="Shabbir Ahmad Usmani">Shabbir Ahmad Usmani</a>, a respected Deobandi <i>alim</i> (scholar) who occupied the position of Shaykh al-Islam in Pakistan in 1949, and <a href="/wiki/Abul_A%27la_Maududi" title="Abul A&#39;la Maududi">Maulana Mawdudi</a> of <a href="/wiki/Jamaat-e-Islami" title="Jamaat-e-Islami">Jamaat-i-Islami</a> played a pivotal role in the demand for an Islamic constitution. <a href="/wiki/Abul_A%27la_Maududi" title="Abul A&#39;la Maududi">Mawdudi</a> demanded that the Constituent Assembly make an explicit declaration affirming the "supreme sovereignty of God" and the supremacy of the <i>shariah</i> in Pakistan.<sup id="cite_ref-98" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-98">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>A significant result of the efforts of the Jamaat-i-Islami and the <i><a href="/wiki/Ulama" title="Ulama">ulama</a></i> was the passage of the <a href="/wiki/Objectives_Resolution" title="Objectives Resolution">Objectives Resolution</a> in March 1949. The Objectives Resolution, which <a href="/wiki/Liaquat_Ali_Khan" title="Liaquat Ali Khan">Liaquat Ali Khan</a> called the second most important step in Pakistan's history, declared that "sovereignty over the entire universe belongs to God Almighty alone and the authority which He has delegated to the State of Pakistan through its people for being exercised within the limits prescribed by Him is a sacred trust". The Objectives Resolution has been incorporated as a preamble to the constitutions of 1956, 1962, and 1973.<sup id="cite_ref-:13_99-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:13-99">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Democracy_in_Pakistan" title="Democracy in Pakistan">Democracy</a> was stalled by the <a href="/wiki/1958_Pakistani_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat" title="1958 Pakistani coup d&#39;état">martial law</a> that had been enforced by President <a href="/wiki/Iskander_Mirza" class="mw-redirect" title="Iskander Mirza">Iskander Mirza</a>, who was replaced by the <a href="/wiki/Commander-in-Chief_of_the_Pakistan_Army" title="Commander-in-Chief of the Pakistan Army">Commander-in-Chief of the Pakistan Army</a>, General <a href="/wiki/Ayub_Khan_(President_of_Pakistan)" class="mw-redirect" title="Ayub Khan (President of Pakistan)">Ayub Khan</a>. After adopting a <a href="/wiki/Constitution_of_Pakistan_of_1962" title="Constitution of Pakistan of 1962">presidential system</a> in 1962, the country experienced exceptional growth until a <a href="/wiki/Indo-Pakistani_War_of_1965" title="Indo-Pakistani War of 1965">second war</a> with India in 1965 that led to an economic downturn and wide-scale <a href="/wiki/Tashkent_Agreement" class="mw-redirect" title="Tashkent Agreement">public disapproval</a> in 1967.<sup id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ChowdhuryMahmud2008_101-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ChowdhuryMahmud2008-101">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Legal_Framework_Order,_1970" title="Legal Framework Order, 1970">Consolidating</a> control from Ayub Khan in 1969, President <a href="/wiki/Yahya_Khan" title="Yahya Khan">Yahya Khan</a> had to deal with a devastating <a href="/wiki/1970_Bhola_cyclone" title="1970 Bhola cyclone">cyclone</a> that caused 500,000 deaths in <a href="/wiki/East_Pakistan" title="East Pakistan">East Pakistan</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1970 Pakistan held its <a href="/wiki/1970_Pakistani_general_election" title="1970 Pakistani general election">first democratic elections</a> since independence, meant to mark a transition from <a href="/wiki/Legal_Framework_Order,_1970" title="Legal Framework Order, 1970">military rule</a> to democracy, but after the East Pakistani <a href="/wiki/Awami_League" title="Awami League">Awami League</a> won against the <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Peoples_Party" class="mw-redirect" title="Pakistan Peoples Party">Pakistan Peoples Party</a> (PPP), Yahya Khan and the military establishment refused to hand over power.<sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Jahan_104-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Jahan-104">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Operation_Searchlight" title="Operation Searchlight">Operation Searchlight</a>, a military crackdown on the Bengali nationalist movement, led to a declaration of independence and the waging of <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh_Liberation_War" title="Bangladesh Liberation War">a war of liberation</a> by the Bengali <a href="/wiki/Mukti_Bahini" title="Mukti Bahini">Mukti Bahini</a> forces in East Pakistan,<sup id="cite_ref-Jahan_104-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Jahan-104">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-105">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup> which in West Pakistan was described as a civil war as opposed to a war of liberation.<sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ayubkhanandbhutto.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Ayubkhanandbhutto.jpg/170px-Ayubkhanandbhutto.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="263" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Ayubkhanandbhutto.jpg/255px-Ayubkhanandbhutto.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Ayubkhanandbhutto.jpg/340px-Ayubkhanandbhutto.jpg 2x" data-file-width="500" data-file-height="774" /></a><figcaption>Signing of the <a href="/wiki/Tashkent_Declaration" title="Tashkent Declaration">Tashkent Declaration</a> to end <a href="/wiki/Indo-Pakistani_War_of_1965" title="Indo-Pakistani War of 1965">hostilities</a> with India in 1965 in <a href="/wiki/Tashkent" title="Tashkent">Tashkent</a>, <a href="/wiki/Union_of_Soviet_Socialist_Republics_(USSR)" class="mw-redirect" title="Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR)">USSR</a>, by President <a href="/wiki/Field_Marshal_Ayub_Khan" class="mw-redirect" title="Field Marshal Ayub Khan">Ayub</a> alongside <a href="/wiki/Zulfikar_Ali_Bhutto" title="Zulfikar Ali Bhutto">Bhutto</a> (centre) and <a href="/wiki/Aziz_Ahmed_(civil_servant)" title="Aziz Ahmed (civil servant)">Aziz Ahmed</a> (left)</figcaption></figure>
<p>Independent researchers estimate that between 300,000 and 500,000 civilians died during this period while the Bangladesh government puts the number of dead at three million,<sup id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup> a figure that is now nearly universally regarded as excessively inflated.<sup id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-108">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup> Some academics such as <a href="/wiki/Rudolph_Rummel" title="Rudolph Rummel">Rudolph Rummel</a> and <a href="/wiki/Rounaq_Jahan" title="Rounaq Jahan">Rounaq Jahan</a> say both sides<sup id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-109">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup> committed genocide; others such as <a href="/wiki/John_Richard_Sisson" title="John Richard Sisson">Richard Sisson</a> and Leo E. Rose believe there was no genocide.<sup id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-110">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup> In response to India's support for the insurgency in East Pakistan, <a href="/wiki/Preemptive_strikes" class="mw-redirect" title="Preemptive strikes">preemptive strikes</a> on India by Pakistan's <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Air_Force" title="Pakistan Air Force">air force</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Navy" title="Pakistan Navy">navy</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Marines" title="Pakistan Marines">marines</a> sparked <a href="/wiki/Indo-Pakistani_War_of_1971" title="Indo-Pakistani War of 1971">a conventional war</a> in 1971 that resulted in an Indian victory and East Pakistan gaining <a href="/wiki/Independence_of_Bangladesh" title="Independence of Bangladesh">independence</a> as <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh" title="Bangladesh">Bangladesh</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Jahan_104-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Jahan-104">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>With Pakistan <a href="/wiki/Instrument_of_Surrender_(1971)" class="mw-redirect" title="Instrument of Surrender (1971)">surrendering</a> in the war, Yahya Khan was replaced by <a href="/wiki/Zulfikar_Ali_Bhutto" title="Zulfikar Ali Bhutto">Zulfikar Ali Bhutto</a> as president; the country worked towards promulgating <a href="/wiki/Constitution_of_Pakistan" title="Constitution of Pakistan">its constitution</a> and putting the country on the road to democracy. Democratic rule resumed from 1972 to 1977—an era of self-consciousness, intellectual <a href="/wiki/Socialism_in_Pakistan" title="Socialism in Pakistan">leftism</a>, <a href="/wiki/Nationalism_in_Pakistan" class="mw-redirect" title="Nationalism in Pakistan">nationalism</a>, and nationwide reconstruction.<sup id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-111">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup> In 1972 Pakistan embarked on an ambitious plan to develop its <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_and_its_Nuclear_Deterrent_Program" class="mw-redirect" title="Pakistan and its Nuclear Deterrent Program">nuclear deterrence</a> capability with <a href="/wiki/Mutually_assured_destruction" class="mw-redirect" title="Mutually assured destruction">the goal of preventing</a> any <a href="/wiki/Foreign_interventionism" class="mw-redirect" title="Foreign interventionism">foreign invasion</a>; the country's <a href="/wiki/KANUPP" class="mw-redirect" title="KANUPP">first</a> <a href="/wiki/Nuclear_power_plant" title="Nuclear power plant">nuclear power plant</a> was inaugurated in that same year.<sup id="cite_ref-112" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-112">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Hoodbhoy_113-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Hoodbhoy-113">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup> Accelerated in response to India's <a href="/wiki/Operation_Smiling_Buddha" class="mw-redirect" title="Operation Smiling Buddha">first nuclear test</a> in 1974, this <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_and_Nuclear_Weapons" class="mw-redirect" title="Pakistan and Nuclear Weapons">crash program</a> was completed in 1979.<sup id="cite_ref-Hoodbhoy_113-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Hoodbhoy-113">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Democracy ended with a <a href="/wiki/Operation_Fair_Play" class="mw-redirect" title="Operation Fair Play">military coup</a> in 1977 against the <a href="/wiki/Socialism_in_Pakistan" title="Socialism in Pakistan">leftist</a> PPP, which saw <a href="/wiki/General_Zia-ul-Haq" class="mw-redirect" title="General Zia-ul-Haq">General Zia-ul-Haq</a> become the president in 1978. From 1977 to 1988, President Zia's <a href="/wiki/Corporate_sector_of_Pakistan" title="Corporate sector of Pakistan">corporatisation</a> and <a href="/wiki/Islamization_of_Economy" class="mw-redirect" title="Islamization of Economy">economic Islamisation</a> initiatives led to Pakistan becoming one of the fastest-growing economies in South Asia.<sup id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-114">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup> While building up the country's <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_and_its_Nuclear_Deterrent_Program" class="mw-redirect" title="Pakistan and its Nuclear Deterrent Program">nuclear program</a>, increasing <a href="/wiki/Zia-ul-Haq%27s_Islamization" class="mw-redirect" title="Zia-ul-Haq&#39;s Islamization">Islamisation</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-115">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup> and the rise of a homegrown <a href="/wiki/Conservatism_in_Pakistan" title="Conservatism in Pakistan">conservative</a> philosophy, Pakistan helped subsidise and distribute US <a href="/wiki/Operation_Cyclone" title="Operation Cyclone">resources to factions</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Afghan_mujahideen" class="mw-redirect" title="Afghan mujahideen">mujahideen</a> against the <a href="/wiki/Soviet_Union" title="Soviet Union">USSR</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War" title="Soviet–Afghan War">intervention</a> in <a href="/wiki/Communist_Afghanistan" class="mw-redirect" title="Communist Afghanistan">communist Afghanistan</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-116" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-116">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup> Pakistan's <a href="/wiki/Khyber_Pakhtunkhwa" title="Khyber Pakhtunkhwa">North-West Frontier Province</a> became a base for the anti-Soviet Afghan fighters, with the province's influential <a href="/wiki/Deobandi" class="mw-redirect" title="Deobandi">Deobandi</a> ulama playing a significant role in encouraging and organising the 'jihad'.<sup id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-117">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Death_of_Muhammad_Zia-ul-Haq" title="Death of Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq">President Zia died</a> in a plane crash in 1988, and <a href="/wiki/Benazir_Bhutto" title="Benazir Bhutto">Benazir Bhutto</a>, daughter of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, was elected as the country's <a href="/wiki/Women_in_Muslim_societies" class="mw-redirect" title="Women in Muslim societies">first female</a> Prime Minister. The PPP was followed by conservative <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Muslim_League_(N)" title="Pakistan Muslim League (N)">Pakistan Muslim League (N)</a>, and over the next decade the leaders of the two parties fought for power, alternating in office while the country's situation worsened; economic indicators fell sharply, in contrast to the 1980s. This period is marked by prolonged <a href="/wiki/Periods_of_stagflation_in_Pakistan" title="Periods of stagflation in Pakistan">stagflation</a>, instability, <a href="/wiki/Corruption_in_Pakistan" title="Corruption in Pakistan">corruption</a>, <a href="/wiki/Nationalism_in_Pakistan" class="mw-redirect" title="Nationalism in Pakistan">nationalism</a>, <a href="/wiki/Geostrategy" title="Geostrategy">geopolitical</a> rivalry with India, and the clash of <a href="/wiki/Socialism_in_Pakistan" title="Socialism in Pakistan">left wing</a>-<a href="/wiki/Conservatism_in_Pakistan" title="Conservatism in Pakistan">right wing</a> ideologies.<sup id="cite_ref-118" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-118">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup> As <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Muslim_League_(N)" title="Pakistan Muslim League (N)">PML (N)</a> secured a <a href="/wiki/Supermajority" title="Supermajority">supermajority</a> in <a href="/wiki/1997_Pakistani_general_election" title="1997 Pakistani general election">elections</a> in 1997, Nawaz Sharif authorised <a href="/wiki/List_of_nuclear_weapons_tests_of_Pakistan" title="List of nuclear weapons tests of Pakistan">nuclear testings</a> (See:<i><a href="/wiki/Chagai-I" title="Chagai-I">Chagai-I</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Chagai-II" title="Chagai-II">Chagai-II</a></i>), as a <a href="/wiki/Tit-for-tat" class="mw-redirect" title="Tit-for-tat">retaliation</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Pokhran-II" title="Pokhran-II">second nuclear tests</a> ordered by India, led by Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Atal_Bihari_Vajpayee" title="Atal Bihari Vajpayee">Atal Bihari Vajpayee</a> in May 1998.<sup id="cite_ref-Stanford_University_Press_119-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stanford_University_Press-119">&#91;115&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Musharaff_and_Bush_in_Islamabad_(cropped).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Musharaff_and_Bush_in_Islamabad_%28cropped%29.jpg/220px-Musharaff_and_Bush_in_Islamabad_%28cropped%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Musharaff_and_Bush_in_Islamabad_%28cropped%29.jpg/330px-Musharaff_and_Bush_in_Islamabad_%28cropped%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/83/Musharaff_and_Bush_in_Islamabad_%28cropped%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="400" data-file-height="300" /></a><figcaption>President <a href="/wiki/George_W._Bush" title="George W. Bush">George W. Bush</a> meets with President <a href="/wiki/Pervez_Musharraf" title="Pervez Musharraf">Musharraf</a> in <a href="/wiki/Islamabad" title="Islamabad">Islamabad</a> during his 2006 visit to Pakistan.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Military tension between the two countries in the <a href="/wiki/Kargil_district" title="Kargil district">Kargil district</a> led to the <a href="/wiki/Kargil_War" title="Kargil War">Kargil War</a> of 1999, and turmoil in <a href="/wiki/Civil-military_relations" class="mw-redirect" title="Civil-military relations">civic-military relations</a> allowed General <a href="/wiki/Pervez_Musharraf" title="Pervez Musharraf">Pervez Musharraf</a> to take over through a <a href="/wiki/1999_Pakistani_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat" title="1999 Pakistani coup d&#39;état">bloodless coup d'état</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-kargil_120-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-kargil-120">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-121" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-121">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup> Musharraf governed Pakistan as <a href="/wiki/Head_of_government" title="Head of government">chief executive</a> from 1999 to 2001 and as President from 2001 to 2008—a period of <a href="/wiki/Enlightened_moderation" title="Enlightened moderation">enlightenment</a>, social <a href="/wiki/Liberal_islam" class="mw-redirect" title="Liberal islam">liberalism</a>, extensive <a href="/wiki/Economic_reforms_in_Pakistan" class="mw-redirect" title="Economic reforms in Pakistan">economic reforms</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-122" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-122">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Pakistan%27s_role_in_the_War_on_Terror" title="Pakistan&#39;s role in the War on Terror">direct involvement in the US-led war on terrorism</a>. When the <a href="/wiki/National_Assembly_(Pakistan)" class="mw-redirect" title="National Assembly (Pakistan)">National Assembly</a> historically completed its first full five-year term on 15 November 2007, the new elections were called by the <a href="/wiki/Election_Commission_of_Pakistan" title="Election Commission of Pakistan">Election Commission</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-123" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-123">&#91;119&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the <a href="/wiki/Assassination_of_Benazir_Bhutto" title="Assassination of Benazir Bhutto">assassination of Benazir Bhutto</a> in 2007, the PPP secured the <a href="/wiki/Majority" title="Majority">most votes</a> in the <a href="/wiki/2008_Pakistani_general_election" title="2008 Pakistani general election">elections</a> of 2008, appointing party member <a href="/wiki/Yousaf_Raza_Gillani" class="mw-redirect" title="Yousaf Raza Gillani">Yousaf Raza Gillani</a> as Prime Minister.<sup id="cite_ref-124" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-124">&#91;120&#93;</a></sup> Threatened with <a href="/wiki/Movement_to_impeach_Pervez_Musharraf" class="mw-redirect" title="Movement to impeach Pervez Musharraf">impeachment</a>, President Musharraf resigned on 18 August 2008, and was succeeded by <a href="/wiki/Asif_Ali_Zardari" title="Asif Ali Zardari">Asif Ali Zardari</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-125" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-125">&#91;121&#93;</a></sup> Clashes with the <a href="/wiki/Judiciary_of_Pakistan" title="Judiciary of Pakistan">judicature</a> prompted <a href="/wiki/Yousaf_Raza_Gillani" class="mw-redirect" title="Yousaf Raza Gillani">Gillani</a>'s disqualification from the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Pakistan" title="Parliament of Pakistan">Parliament</a> and as the <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Pakistan" title="Prime Minister of Pakistan">Prime Minister</a> in June 2012.<sup id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-126">&#91;122&#93;</a></sup> By its own financial calculations, Pakistan's <a href="/wiki/Pakistan%27s_role_in_the_War_on_Terror" title="Pakistan&#39;s role in the War on Terror">involvement in the war on terrorism</a> has cost up to $118&#160;billion,<sup id="cite_ref-127" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-127">&#91;123&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/List_of_terrorist_incidents_in_Pakistan_since_2001" title="List of terrorist incidents in Pakistan since 2001">sixty thousand casualties</a> and more than 1.8&#160;million displaced civilians.<sup id="cite_ref-128" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-128">&#91;124&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/2013_Pakistani_general_election" title="2013 Pakistani general election">general election</a> held in 2013 saw the PML (N) almost achieve a <a href="/wiki/Supermajority" title="Supermajority">supermajority</a>, following which <a href="/wiki/Nawaz_Sharif" title="Nawaz Sharif">Nawaz Sharif</a> was elected as the Prime Minister, returning to the post for the third time in fourteen years, in a democratic transition.<sup id="cite_ref-129" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-129">&#91;125&#93;</a></sup> In 2018, <a href="/wiki/Imran_Khan" title="Imran Khan">Imran Khan</a> (the chairman of <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Tehreek-e-Insaf" title="Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf">PTI</a>) won the <a href="/wiki/2018_Pakistan_general_election" class="mw-redirect" title="2018 Pakistan general election">2018 Pakistan general election</a> with 116 general seats and became the 22nd <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Pakistan" title="Prime Minister of Pakistan">Prime Minister of Pakistan</a> in election of <a href="/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Pakistan" title="National Assembly of Pakistan">National Assembly of Pakistan</a> for <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister" class="mw-redirect" title="Prime Minister">Prime Minister</a> by getting 176 votes against <a href="/wiki/Shehbaz_Sharif" title="Shehbaz Sharif">Shehbaz Sharif</a> (the chairman of <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Muslim_League_(N)" title="Pakistan Muslim League (N)">PML (N)</a>) who got 96 votes.<sup id="cite_ref-130" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-130">&#91;126&#93;</a></sup> In April 2022, <a href="/wiki/Shehbaz_Sharif" title="Shehbaz Sharif">Shehbaz Sharif</a> was elected as Pakistan's new prime minister, after Imran Khan lost a no-confidence vote in the parliament.<sup id="cite_ref-131" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-131">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<div style="clear:both;"></div>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Role_of_Islam">Role of Islam</span></h2>
